capitals.name: Kabasa (Cabaça)
capitals.note: Coordinates are the gazetteer's Ndalatando; the page puts Kabasa 'on the highlands near modern N'dalatando'. Sacked by the Portuguese in 1617 when Ngola Mbandi fled to Kindonga, an island in the Kwanza; Nzinga returned to Kabasa in late 1622. [Fix af-06, 2026-10-19: the old note kept Kabasa to 1671 because the seat of the Portuguese-installed kings was unknown; the Ndongo page now read says Hari a Kiluanji was 'lord of the rocky fortress of Mpungo a Ndongo (or Pungo Andongo)' and Filipe ruled Pungo a Ndongo, and the Pungo Andongo page says that town was the capital 'during its last years', so the second entry takes over in 1626.]

capitals.name: Pungo a Ndongo (Pungo Andongo)
capitals.note: APPROXIMATE stand-in: the Pungo Andongo page puts the town in Cacuso municipality, Malanje Province, gives no coordinates, and the gazetteer lacks the name; the point is the cell nearest the centre of the Lukala-side Malanje block of the drawn shape (about 70 km from the town on the author's reading, confidence 1). 'During its last years, this town was the capital of the Kingdom of Ndongo' (Pungo Andongo page); in 1671 the Portuguese took it.

correction.text: the Mbundu highlands 'between the Lukala and Kwanza Rivers': Bengo, Cuanza Norte and the Lukala side of Malanje Province (Pungo Andongo), without the Luanda coast and without Matamba's and Kasanje's Malanje lands

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria has no Ndongo). The page gives no boundary: Ndongo lay in the highlands 'between the Lukala and Kwanza Rivers' with a tenuous hold on Kisama south of the Kwanza, its capital Kabasa near N'dalatando and (1626-1671) its last seat at Pungo a Ndongo in Malanje Province. No area check is possible: the Ndongo page gives no infobox area and Cliopatria has no Ndongo. [Fix af-06, 2026-10-19: the old shape was the gazetteer's 'Ndongo' region (Luanda, Bengo, Cuanza Norte and all of Malanje, 527 cells), which contained the whole of kingdom-of-matamba (Malanje, 305 cells) and kingdom-of-kasanje (118 cells) and 108 cells of portuguese-angola's 1582 shape. The new shape is Bengo (minus the Cliopatria Kongo shape of 1662, which the old region also overlapped by 34 cells), Cuanza Norte and the Lukala side of Malanje (Malanje within 50 km of the Lucala river, where the Pungo Andongo page puts the last capital); the rest of Malanje is Matamba's and Kasanje's. The Luanda coast is left out because portuguese-angola founds Luanda in 1575 from 'nobody'.]

ledger.note: 1518: Ngola Kiluanji sends ambassadors to Portugal; the infobox 'Established' date for Ndongo. Founder 'Ngola Kiluanje (also Ngola Inene), described as a migrant from Kongo'; the page calls Ndongo 'one of multiple vassal states to Kongo, though Ndongo was the most powerful' and notes 'Angola' among the Kongo king's titles in 1535. The year is the page's, the land is the gazetteer's Ndongo region. [Fix af-06, 2026-10-19: region redrawn without Matamba and Kasanje (see keyframe 0). The Ambundu page puts the end of Kongo's authority in 1556 ('this led to war, in which the Bakongo were defeated in 1556') while the Ndongo page calls that independence claim 'a misreading of the sources' and dates no end of the Kongo link; the page the reviewer named (Ngola Kiluanji) does not exist under that title, so the end of the vassalage stays undated.]

region.text: Kabasa, the capital, 'on the highlands near modern N'dalatando'

ledger.note: 1617: Governor Luis Mendes de Vasconcelos 'sacked the capital' and forced Ngola Mbandi to flee to Kindonga. The Imbangala-backed Portuguese assault of 1617-1618 is the Imbangala page's 'Luis Mendes de Vasconcelos's 1618 assault on Ndongo'.

region.text: Kabasa, the capital, 'on the highlands near modern N'dalatando'

ledger.note: 1622: peace after Nzinga's embassy. 'A peace treaty was subsequently agreed upon, and Nzinga returned to Kabasa in triumph in late 1622' (Nzinga page); the Ndongo page: Mbandi sent his sister to negotiate a treaty in 1621.

1626: the Portuguese install a rival king. 'The Portuguese governor Fernão de Sousa installed Hari a Kiluanji as a rival king' (Hari died in a smallpox epidemic and was replaced by Filipe Hari a Ngola); the Portuguese had declared war on Nzinga on 15 March 1626 and by late 1628 her army was down to about 200 men (Nzinga page). Ndongo now continues as a Portuguese client under Hari and Filipe while Nzinga rules from Matamba (1631); the vassal tint is the suzerain's to record (portuguese-angola with counterpart kingdom-of-ndongo). [Fix af-06, 2026-10-19: the vassal_start that mirrors portuguese-angola's follows as the next event (the page does not use the word 'vassal' or 'client'; it says Filipe 'served the Portuguese loyally'); confidence 2.]

region.text: the client kingdom of Hari a Kiluanji and Filipe Hari a Ngola, 'lord of the rocky fortress of Mpungo a Ndongo'

ledger.note: 1626: Ndongo becomes a Portuguese client under Hari a Kiluanji. 'The Portuguese governor Fernão de Sousa installed Hari a Kiluanji as a rival king' (the sobas he convened re-elected Hari, 'lord of the rocky fortress of Mpungo a Ndongo'); Filipe Hari a Ngola succeeded him and 'served the Portuguese loyally'. The vassal tint is drawn by portuguese-angola's vassal_start of 1626 (counterpart kingdom-of-ndongo); the List of Ngolas page calls both kings 'usurpers imposed upon the people by the Portuguese'. [Fix af-06, 2026-10-19: added as the mirror the reviewer asked for; the old rename stayed and this sits beside it.]

1626: the seat moves to Pungo a Ndongo. The Ndongo page names Hari a Kiluanji 'lord of the rocky fortress of Mpungo a Ndongo (or Pungo Andongo)' and the Pungo Andongo page says that town was 'the capital of the Kingdom of Ndongo' in 'its last years'; the year is the installation of Hari (the pages give no separate date for the move) and the point is a stand-in (identity.capitals).

[Fix af-06, 2026-10-19: zone redrawn as the new Ndongo shape (the old zone was the gazetteer's Ndongo region, which included Matamba itself).]

wars.name: Portuguese war on Ndongo (Dias de Novais to the 1599 border)
wars.outcome: Ngola Ndambi ambushed Portuguese forces in 1579-1580; a Kongo invasion was 'narrowly defeated in 1580'; the Portuguese founded Massangano in 1582 and were crushed at Kabasa in 1590 after Ndongo allied with Matamba; Ndongo and Portugal formalized their border in 1599.
wars.note: The ambush is Njinga Ndambi in the page's wording. The page names no battle for 1590.

zones.text: Kabasa, the capital, 'on the highlands near modern N'dalatando'

wars.outcome: Kabasa was sacked in 1617 and Ngola Mbandi fled to Kindonga; a peace treaty was negotiated in 1621-1622 and Nzinga returned to Kabasa in late 1622.

wars.name: Nzinga's wars against Portugal

zones.text: the Mbundu highlands of Ndongo that Nzinga reclaimed in 1641-1644

wars.outcome: The Portuguese declared war on Nzinga on 15 March 1626 and installed Hari a Kiluanji; she fled in 1627-1628, took Matamba in 1631, reclaimed large parts of Ndongo with Dutch help in 1641-1644, won at Kombi in 1647; peace in late 1656 and a treaty of 1657 recognizing her as queen of Ndongo and Matamba.

wars.name: Revolt of Filipe Hari a Ngola

zones.text: the Mbundu highlands of Ndongo around Pungo a Ndongo

wars.outcome: Filipe revolted against the Portuguese; his fortress fell in 1671 and Ndongo ended as an independent kingdom.

notes: Cliopatria has no Ndongo. The page gives no boundary or area, so the shape is the gazetteer's 'Ndongo' region (aliased 'Ndongo and Matamba, Angola (kingdom core)') at confidence 2, and the Kwanza loss events are 25 km discs. Not settled: the date Ndongo stopped being a Kongo vassal (the Ndongo page rejects the 1556 independence claim as a misreading), the place of the 1590 battle (unnamed), where the 1599 border ran, the seat of the Portuguese-installed kings, Pungo Andongo and the Battle of Ambuíla (not on the pages), and the year Nzinga's Ndongo-Matamba union absorbed the Ndongo lands she reclaimed. The Portuguese-installed regime of Hari and Filipe (1626-1671) is kept inside this dossier as a rename; the portuguese-angola dossier carries the vassal tint (vassal_start 1626, vassal_end 1671, counterpart kingdom-of-ndongo). Capital coordinates come from the gazetteer's Ndalatando. Page budget (new state, 2-5): five pages opened (Ndongo, Nzinga, Matamba, Imbangala, Portuguese Angola), the last two thin. [Fix af-06, 2026-10-19: (1) BLOCKING shape: redrawn as Bengo (minus the Cliopatria Kongo shape), Cuanza Norte and the Lukala side of Malanje (Malanje within 50 km of the Lucala), cut into three keyframes that drop the Luanda coast (1575 is portuguese-angola's founding from 'nobody'), the Massangano corridor (1582) and the Cambambe corridor (1602); Matamba (Malanje minus this block minus the Kwango band) and Kasanje (the Kwango band) no longer lie inside it. The reviewer allowed western Malanje 'if a page supports it': the Pungo Andongo page does (the town was the capital in Ndongo's last years). (2) The 1626 client kingdom now has its vassal_start (counterpart portuguese-angola) and vassal_end 1671 beside the rename, mirroring portuguese-angola ledger 6 and 11. (3) The capital moves to Pungo a Ndongo in 1626 on a stand-in point (the page gives no coordinates). (4) Thin items re-tried: the 1599 border line is still not on the Ndongo page; the end of the Kongo vassalage is undated (the Ngola_Kiluanji page does not exist under that title; the Ambundu page says 1556, the Ndongo page calls that a misreading). Disagreement kept: the Ambundu page says Ndongo was 'defeated by Portugal in 1614', the Ndongo page dates the end to 1671; 1671 stands.]
